title: Keboard manager disabled keys can still be triggered

judgment.rationale: The author confirmed on 0.101.2362 that rapidly pressing two disabled Win shortcuts can leak the second to Windows, and supplied a second deterministic sequence where a disabled Win+3 chord prevents a later valid Win+2 remap while Win remains held. These cases justify a focused engine design, but the exact event transition remains unproven.
evidence: The report gives both rapid Win+1/Win+2 and held-Win valid/disabled/valid sequences.
The author said the behavior persists on 0.101.2362.
The live thread has three comments; no assignee or linked PR was found.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve a focused Keyboard Manager engine investigation and replay both sequences through the native event-stream test surface.

fix_assessment.rationale: No linked upstream fix attempt covers these two sequences. A state/suppression correction may be applicable, but must be tied to the failing event transition rather than assumed from the symptom.

proposed_fixes.title: Keep disabled shortcut suppression and chord reset consistent across consecutive Win chords
proposed_fixes.root_cause: A completed disabled shortcut may leave logical chord or physical modifier bookkeeping inconsistent, allowing the next disabled action key through or preventing the next valid remap. This is a hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause.
plan: Add native event-stream cases for rapid disabled Win+1/Win+2 and held-Win valid Win+1, disabled Win+3, then valid Win+2.
Trace HandleShortcutRemapEvent and ResetChordsIfNeeded across every key-down and key-up in the failing sequence, including the suppression return value and started-chord state.
At the observed failing transition, reset only completed logical chord state while preserving a physically held Win key and suppressing both halves of a disabled action key.
Add regression cases for key-release ordering, valid chained remaps, and injected-event filtering.
verification: Neither rapid disabled shortcut reaches the Windows shell.
A valid remap still fires after a disabled chord while Win remains physically held.
Releasing Win leaves no stuck logical or OS modifier state.

confidence.rationale: The reporter supplied deterministic sequences and the code has a native event-stream test surface, but the precise failing branch still needs a focused trace.

issue_context.summary: Keyboard Manager can leak a disabled Win shortcut after another disabled chord and can leave a later valid Win remap unresponsive until the held Win key is released.
known_information: The rapid disabled-shortcut case was reported on an enterprise machine with Company Portal installation.
The author confirmed the behavior on PowerToys 0.101.2362.
A second example uses valid Win+1 and Win+2 remaps plus disabled Win+3 while Win is kept held.
The existing public artifact records #25311 and #47839 as related but distinct reports.
inferences: The two sequences may share an inconsistent logical-chord or suppression transition.
The appropriate investigation is in runtime event handling, not the shortcut editor.
issue_context.analysis: The reporter's concrete sequences are sufficient for a maintainer-side event replay, so another generic information request would not reduce uncertainty. The current source contains HandleShortcutRemapEvent and ResetChordsIfNeeded, and OSLevelShortcutRemappingTests.cpp is the focused native test surface; no root cause is confirmed.
initial_investigation: Read the complete issue body and all three live comments, including the 0.101.2362 confirmation and held-modifier sequence.
Checked current labels, assignees, linked work, and references to related reports.

Inspected KeyboardManagerEngineLibrary/KeyboardEventHandlers.cpp and KeyboardManagerEngineTest/OSLevelShortcutRemappingTests.cpp; existing tests cover other event-order scenarios but not these exact sequences.

design.title: Keep disabled shortcut suppression and chord reset consistent across consecutive Win chords

reproduce.title: Trace consecutive disabled Win shortcut event ordering
prerequisites: Current upstream main or a matching current build
A native test or debug build that can record keyboard-hook event order
steps: Configure Win+1 and Win+2 as disabled and verify each individually.
Press Win+1 and then Win+2 rapidly; record whether either shell action occurs.
Configure valid Win+1 and Win+2 remaps plus disabled Win+3.
Keep Win held, press 1, then 3, then 2 without releasing Win; record each hook event, suppression result, and chord state.
reproduce.expected_result: Disabled shortcuts never reach Windows, and valid Win+2 still executes after disabled Win+3 without releasing Win.
